attribution: Adi Shankaracharya; one of the independent works whose attribution scholars generally accept
author: shankara
period: Traditionally 8th century CE; scholars generally place Shankara in the 7th–8th centuries
summary: 'A thousand teachings': a two-part manual on how to teach Advaita, in prose and in verse, and widely considered an authentic independent work of Shankara.
whyRead: Because its authorship is well accepted, scholars use the Upadesha Sahasri as a reliable guide to Shankara's own thought, alongside his commentaries. The prose part is unusual in describing how a teacher should instruct a student step by step.
questions: How should the Self be taught?
What is the relation between the Self and the mind's contents?
Why is action no remedy for ignorance?

keyTeachings.title: A method of teaching
keyTeachings.text: The prose part presents dialogues showing how a teacher guides a qualified student from identification with the body to recognition of the Self.

keyTeachings.title: The Self as pure consciousness
keyTeachings.text: The Self is presented as consciousness that illumines the mind's modifications while remaining unchanged by them.

keyTeachings.title: Knowledge versus action
keyTeachings.text: It argues that because bondage is ignorance, only knowledge ends it, and action, which presupposes the distinction of doer and deed, cannot.

relatedTexts.note: A popular work traditionally attributed to Shankara, whose authorship is more doubtful
